prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and import competition shift labour demand and shape wage structure and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B006 as a single part with Autor, Hanson and Katz. I re-tested it against the chair's questions and not against the count of supporters. Ten of eleven files agree, but that is convergence and not evidence, and several of us moved after reading the openings. The question is whether the case survives on the common criteria. I think it does, for three reasons. First, the question is central: who bears the costs of technological and trade change, and how persistent those costs are. Second, it pairs a framework (the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium, task content) with designs whose identifying assumptions are explicit and have been tested by replication and critique for a decade or more. Third, the work reaches labour, trade, macro and policy, and the files describe the debate as about magnitude and persistence, not about whether the effects exist. On the third laureate I keep Katz. His wage-structure and skill-demand work is an independent strand that Autor and Hanson do not carry, and it supplies the interpretive frame that makes the trade evidence a statement about labour demand and not only about local adjustment. I would draft the citation as one discovery: how technological change and import competition shift labour demand and the adjustment of wages and local labour markets. It would not claim origination of the task model, would not restate the 2023 or 2024 citations, and would not assert a settled long-run magnitude. I treat Dorn's exclusion as a real cost of the three-name cap, not as a judgment about the quality of his contribution.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weakest point. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is cut only by the cap. Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu's task-model theory lie outside the credited names. Katz's best-known education-technology work is with Goldin, so his marginal claim is the most exposed of the three, and I accept that Strömberg and Teorell describe it that way. The set may read as two adjacent lines joined by an outcome, and a committee that wants a single design-based discovery could reasonably choose Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The shift-share inference concerns and the persistence of the China-shock effects are not resolved. B007 has cleaner credit, which is a genuine advantage over B006. I weigh it below B006 mainly on identification of the cross-country evidence and on timing relative to the 2024 prize. I cannot claim that weighing is free of judgment.

responses.point: Friberg is the only member preferring B007 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley). He ranks B006 sixth and would credit only Autor and Hanson, because he reads B006 as two lines and Katz's work as partly overlapping the Goldin prize. He accepts that identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is the weak flank.
responses.response: I take your B007 case seriously, and I agree with you that the 2024 prize was a different agenda, as I said in round 1. I also accept that the Persson and Tabellini credit is cleaner than anything in B006. Where I differ is the weight on identification. By your own account the headline cross-country results are sensitive to specification, while the B006 designs have faced direct replication tests. On the two-name set, I think it drops the skill-demand account that explains why the shocks matter for wages, and it turns the prize into a trade-shock award. If the committee wants the narrow version, the honest comparison is Katz against Dorn, not whether to stop at two. I also note your disclosure of the joint price-setting paper with me. I do not think it bears on B007 or B006.

responses.point: Krusell moved B006 to first on the merits. He keeps Katz over Dorn because Katz anchors the long-run skill-demand strand, he treats the adjacent prizes as an attribution and wording matter and not a reason to wait, and he flags B007 as a conflict because Persson is at IIES.
responses.response: I agree with the Katz reasoning, and with your point that the citation can be worded to keep distance from 2023 and 2024. I would add one caveat to your framing of attribution. If Katz's separate claim is only argued through the Goldin work, it is the weakest link, so the committee should rest it on the wage-structure and skill-premium line that predates it. On B007 I note that Persson is also at my home institute, so I disclose it as well and do not adjudicate it. I do not think the B007 question turns on that shared affiliation. My reason for ranking it below B006 is the strength of identification, and I would hold that view whoever was credited.

responses.point: Strömberg treats B006 as strong, credibly identified work. He calls Katz's marginal claim the most exposed part of the trio, asks whether the committee sees one discovery or two, and names Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the natural fallback within the same discovery.
responses.response: I accept that Katz is the most exposed name, and I think that is the honest centre of this decision. My answer to your coherence question is that one citation can hold both strands if it is framed around labour demand and adjustment. Your fallback is credible, and I would not call it a loss of merit if the committee chose it. I stay with Katz because I judge the skill-premium framework to be a separable achievement, not an add-on. The prize is worded poorly if it gives the trade shock without the demand-side account. If the committee decides the single design-based discovery matters more, I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson and would not treat it as a different prize.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B006 on identification, replication and cross-field reach. He calls Katz's claim the closest call within B006 because of the Goldin overlap. He lists B004 and B007 as alternatives, and he warns that the 2023 and 2024 prizes may reduce the marginal case.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap is the best argument against my own preferred option, and I accept your assessment that Katz is the closest call. I do not think it is a duplication of a prize. The 2023 and 2024 citations were about women's labour-market outcomes and about institutions and prosperity, and neither recognised the empirical task approach or the evidence on trade exposure. Where I would ask more of the committee is the drafting. The citation should say what B006 adds, namely evidence on adjustment to technology and trade. It should avoid the education-technology race as such. I also agree with you that B004 has the more severe attribution problem. I rank it behind B006 and do not list it as an alternative.

responses.point: Andersson moved from B004 to B006 because the credit map for Autor, Hanson and Katz is clearer than any B004 trio. He wants the citation anchored on labour-demand adjustment and not on originating the task model, and he questions how I weighed B032.
responses.response: I agree with your move and with the wording constraint, and I note that it is the same constraint I set in round 1. On B032 I have moved since my opening. I still regard the Kiyotaki and Moore mechanism as foundational with clean credit. But the direct tests of the original model are thin, and the 2022 prize narrows the room, so I keep it only as an alternative. I would not argue it against B006 on the common criteria. I also agree that B004's attribution problem is a real cost. My earlier remark about exposure to the post-2008 and 2021 to 2023 inflation debates was about empirical standing, not about its importance.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn is the better third name. I regard this as a genuine close call between a broader citation and a single design-based one, and I would accept the Dorn variant if the committee prefers it.
Whether the committee reads technology and trade as one discovery or two, and whether one citation can say so without overstating either strand.
How much of Katz's marginal credit survives the Goldin overlap once it is based on the wage-structure and skill-premium line, which I have not independently verified beyond the round-1 files.

Persistence, magnitude and external validity of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share inference concerns. My view is that the finding on labour demand and local adjustment is established while magnitudes are not, which rests on how colleagues describe the literature.
Whether the 2023 and 2024 prizes reduce the marginal case for B006 on timing as opposed to merit, and whether B007's cleaner credit should outweigh B006's broader confirmation.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose, without adjudicating: co-authorship with Boppart and Friberg, IIES colleagueship with Krusell and Boppart, and frequent co-authorship with Krusell (secretary). Persson, credited on B007 (an alternative), is at IIES, my home institute, per Krusell's round-1 disclosure. I wrote the chair's round-1 summary, which is a process record and not a ruling, and I do not use its support counts as merit. My own social-mobility research is topically near B050, which I rank low and do not prefer. My climate-economics work (B-series not on this shortlist) and my 2018 presentation speech do not bear on B006. I have not independently verified any outside source.
